editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: My name is Kristen Miller. Today is June 5, 2002. We're at the Colmery-O'Neil VA Medical Center in Topeka, Kansas, and we have the honor and privilege of having with us today Mr. Glenn Ray Sheridan, who resides at 1242 Southwest Western, in Topeka, Kansas, 66604. Mr. Sheridan was born September 4, 1925, in Neilsville, Minnesota. He served in the Navy. He is a veteran of two wars. World War II, where he served from November 18, 1942, through February 3, 1946. He is also a veteran of the Korean War from March 22, 1951, and he was in the military until March 25, 1955. Due to Mr. Sheridan's distinguished extended service, we will be doing two tapes on Mr. Sheridan. Mr. Sheridan, during his service, received the Good Conduct Medal, the Navy Commendation, American Theater, Asiatic Theater with five Battle Stars, the Army of Occupation in Japan, the Philippine Liberation Medal with two Battle Stars, and the Victory Medal. It is an extreme honor to have Mr. Sheridan with us here today. Mr. Sheridan, would you like to be called Glenn or Mr. Sheridan?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Glenn would sound better, I think.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Okay. The first thing I want to ask you, how did you happen to be in the military?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, the war was on and we just--we just--a bunch of us just decided we wanted to be in it. And so I originally would have went in the army, but the man I enlisted with had been in the North Dakota National Guard and he didn't want to go back into the army, so he--he--we were going to go into the Marine Corps. We went to Grand Forks, North Dakota, to enlist. And they had a 30-day waiting period. So a Navy man walked down the hall and so he said you guys want to go in right away? And we said we did. And so he said well, he said, we can take you in the Navy right away. I said well, I said I want to be in something where I--where I can shoot. Because I considered myself a very good shot. And he said, well, he said, we can make you a gunner's mate. And he said, that way you'll get--you know, you'll be able to do that. So he convinced me and the young man I was going in with, so we went in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: How old were you?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I was just--I had just turned 17 in September.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: So did your parents sign for you?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes, my dad signed for me. When I asked him, he said--he says I'll be glad to sign for you because, he said, I was not able to go in during World War I. So he said, I've always regretted that. And he said, I think it's really right that you do go. So I did go in. And then after I went in, too, my brothers later went in, also into the Navy.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: So there were three of you serving--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: In World War II, yes.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --in World War II. What did your father do for a living?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: He was a farmer.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: So of course it really hurt, I think, all of us being gone while he was farming. 'Cause he was a pretty big farmer back there. And I don't think there we get hired help because everybody--you know, three of us should have been helping him farm. But the war was on on and that was a higher priority.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Were you the first of the three boys--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --to go in? And were there other children in the family?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I had three sisters and three brothers.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: So there were four of us boys. And my youngest brother went in then during the Korean War.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: He went in the Army.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Okay. Where did you report to first for basic or--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: First place I reported to was--I think Fargo, North Dakota. And the man put his hand behind my back and in front of the guy I enlisted with, we were standing in single file. And my service number was 6398631, and his service number was 6398632. And he ended up in Farragut, Idaho, and I went to Great Lakes, Illinois. So while I was in Great Lakes, I--I didn't know he had gotten to Farragut and I looked all over for him, but I couldn't find him. One day--one day I was running around looking for him and I was--instead of walking I was running and a young ensign stopped me. He said you're in the Navy now, you can't run back and forth, you can't run, you got to walk. So he took my name, and for that weekend I had extra duty. I had to wash all the windows in a great big building. And windows were 6 by 4. And so I started on top and I washed windows all day Saturday and all day Sunday. I didn't quite finish. So on Monday--Monday afternoon when training was over I went back to finish and he said--the guy said what are you doing here? I said--I said I want to--I got to finish these windows, I didn't get them all washed this weekend. He said you're crazy, he said, that was extra duty for the weekend, you don't have to do that. So I couldn't understand it. Because at the farm you finished a project, you know. So that was my first lesson in the Navy, I guess.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: How else did you find basic training?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: It was--for me it was pretty easy. I was--I was--I tried to be a good athlete and I was in pretty good shape. So physically it was very good. And I had gone away to a school in Crookston, I had gone to a Farmer AC it's called, agricultural college, because there was never no high school locally, very close to us. So I was used to being with other people. So basic was very easy for me.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: How was it being away from home?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, I think the fact that I had gone to the AC for one semester helped that too. I didn't get very homesick. I couldn't--I just couldn't believe you didn't--you didn't have to go out and milk 13 cows when the day was over.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: When you completed your basic training, what were your orders?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, then we went to a school, we went to schools then after that. And then right during--I think during the last part of basic, we had to sign up for whatever school we were trying to get, so I signed up for gunner's mate. And then I also heard that if you put a big C on your application card, you would get--you would get armed--you would get armed guard duty, which was--armed guard duty meant you would be on a--a gunner's mate on a merchant vessel or a troop ship. So I had done that and neither one of them worked. I ended up being a pharmacist's mate.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Why did they decide to make you a pharmacist's mate, and what did you think of that?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I didn't like it very good. And I don't know how they did it. I used to sometimes think well, maybe because my dad was a farmer, I was probably a pharmacist. I didn't know much about, you know, anything with--about whatever even that was. And so I had to go to a hospital corps school, and that was done right at Great Lakes. And they had different instructors come in. And one--in one of the sessions, why, we had to give shots. So we'd give distilled water to each other. And the fellow I was with, he said I'll squirt mine on the floor if you squirt yours on the floor. So we did, and we didn't give each other a shot. So that's how I got by with that. And then other things they were teaching us what we would have to do. One time they--the nurse come in and showed us an enema can, and said we would probably--we would probably have to learn how to give an enema. So she said this was a can and then it had a big long hose with it. And she said--she said you put whatever it is in there and then you heat it with water and you get--give the enema. I had never heard of an enema before. And I--I--I guess I just remembered what she said and that was about all I ever did remember. After we graduated, we went to--I went to the Philadelphia Navy Hospital. And while I was a corpsman on the--at the hospital, I was on what they call SOQ 11, sick officers quarters on the 11th floor. And one of the admirals that was a patient there would get a warm oil enema. He'd get a hot oil enema every night. So I had--I was getting by real well. We were on day duty and we'd be done about 9 o'clock at night. And I--I avoided giving anybody any enemas until finally this nurse said it's your turn to give one today. And I said well, I don't know how. She said well, you learned that in corps school. And I said well, I never done it yet. She said what you do is you ___+ {Interview interrupted by a knock on the door.} So I asked the nurse, I said well how do I really--how do I mix this? She said well, you put some oil in the can, and then she said, you put it in water and put water in it. I thought she meant put water in the can. And I said how hot should the water be? She said well, it should be hot. She was busy, she didn't have a lot of time to tell me I think. So I just put some oil in the can, and put a bunch of hot water in it. And I went down to the head that admiral--the admiral would be in. And I know that the water was hot because I could see it steaming. And I opened the door to the head and the admiral was in there, and the door was shut on his commode, he was in there. And I said admiral, your enema is ready. And he said all right son, he said, just hand the tube underneath, he said. And I did. And then he said okay, turn it on. I turned it on, I heard the loudest racket. He really yelled hard. And I ran out of the head, and I was carrying this enema can and about ten feet of hose, and it was going through the ward and it was steaming out of the hose and water was squirting out. So the next day then I got transferred to the TB ward. No more wards in there. But I would say that when I was on the SOQ ward, I met a colonel, an army colonel who was paralyzed from the neck down. And we'd have to hold his cigarette so he could smoke them, and we'd have to hold the paper so he could read it. And every day we'd have to move him a little bit because of the bed sores. Just turn him like a quarter of a degree or, you know, just roll him over a little bit. And this add--this colonel wanted us to kill him. He had been laying in there--he just didn't--wanted to end his life. And of course when he'd say that, it would scare the Dickens out of all of us, you know, because no way were we going to kill anybody over there. But the colonel would talk to us. And he said he had been in France in World War I and he had the--he had the big--he had the Congressional Medal. And he had had a big parade for him on Market Street in Philadelphia. And from his--his window you could see Market Street. And he was--he said he was so proud, he said, his wife and three daughters come up and seen him every day. He was very proud of that. And he said pretty soon it was once a week. Pretty soon once a month. And then while I was there, it had been 7 years since he had seen them. So he really didn't feel he had very much to live for. But I learned a lesson there though that when I--I thought if I get my chance in combat, I'll going to make sure if it looks like I'm paralyzed, I'm going to have somebody--somebody do me in. Because I didn't want to spend it like the Colonel. But after--after this mishap with the--with the enema and I got transferred to the TB ward, it was a whole different ball game. I was on night duty also. They put me on the worst job I could get. And maybe it was good because at least I wasn't--didn't see the admiral any more. But while I was on this--this TB ward, one thing I remember was we had a man that we had--he had TB real bad and he also had asthma. He was very, very thin. And he had a--he had PRM, prescription whenever he needed it, for adrenaline hydrochloride. When he'd have a coughing spell. So I--so he came to the desk one night and he--and he--and he said I got a PRN up there, he said, from some adrenal hydrochloride. He said I need a shot right now. So I opened up the narcot--the medicine chest and got the needle and got everything ready. And I used the alcohol sponge and I sponged him down. And I just could not penetrate his skin with that needle. It was just like in basic--in early--I'd squirt it on the floor and the other guy did too. I just--I just couldn't do it. And the guy who was getting the--supposed to get the shot said by god, you can't do it, he said I'll do it. And he shot it in his arm. And when he did, the needle broke. And I think he got most of the shot all right, but the needle broke anyway. And so then we had to--we had to get it off. Get the needle out of his arm. And on that ward, was a doctor whose name was Waterman. And the story was that he was a German citizen. He was not a US citizen, but he was a doctor. And he lived right on--right in the hospital. On the fifth floor. Which was kind of like the operating room. And so they got ahold of Dr. Waterman and he came in. And I had--this guy with the needle in his arm went in there and he cut this needle out. And he told me, you know, he said, very bad. You got to learn how to give these shots. So--so after that I worked with Dr. Waterman quite a lot. There were many times--I mean, I got to know him. And he--I got to know him later because there was a big train wreck in Philadelphia. And I think 40 some people were killed. And all the hospitals were full. And so he came to the hospital. And this particular time I was running in the elevator up and down. And the nurse was holding the--holding the bottle of glucose or whatever he was getting. And she was shaking so bad that she would shake the needle out. So this doctor said, you run the elevator and let him hold this bottle. So I held it. And that was the second time I had anything to do with Dr. Waterman. But after that, I got to know him pretty good. There were--there were other times--there was one time we were--I was on a special watch. On a guy who had had a double renal calculus operation, double kidney operation. And they had done the first one and then they done the second one. And they done the second one too soon probably. And so he was in an oxygen tent and he-- he was itching at the staples that they put in. And both incisions gave away, and the stomach come right out on the bed. So I was with Dr. Waterman on that one too. The man didn't survive, but it wasn't because Dr. Waterman didn't try really hard. He really did. But just wasn't, you know, just was a bad thing.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Were you living on base--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --at that time?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes. I was living on base.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: And did you have--did you have leave--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --or what were your hours like?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: It was regular--it was regular--I think on this time I was on night duty, so I would go on at like 9:30 at night and be off at 6:30 in the morning. So I would--I would--but I would have free liberty then whenever I was off.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: When you were off duty, were you in uniform?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes, we were in uniform. I was at the hospital. I was a HN ____+ . It was called a striker, striker rating. And I--I stayed on that job for quite awhile. And then I got a job in the prison ward.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: This is also in--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: In Philadelphia.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --in Philadelphia? Okay.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: In Philadelphia at a Navy prison. A Navy prison. It's a brig unless there's over a thousand inmates, then it becomes a prison. And these prisoners, if they got sick, would come to the hospital. And we had a--we had a room on the seventh floor that had these--that was for these prisoners. We had a Marine guard on the outside of the door. And we had all corpsmen working in there. There were no nurses in there at all. Doctors would make a--make a sick call every other day or something or whenever we felt we needed to have one. Otherwise, it was all by us guys. And if a nurse did come down, it was because we asked them to. So while we were at this ward then, we had--we had a narcotics locker and we had all kinds of things that most of us didn't really know what it was--anything about, you know. By this time I was a senior corpsman, I think I was--I don't believe I was a third class petty officer yet, but I was--I was an HM1. So I was the senior corpsman on this ward. And we would experiment sometimes with patients. We had--we'd take Dexedrine--Dexedrine, which is dextroamphetamine sulphate, and Nembutal, and we'd--we'd--we'd dissolve it in--in distilled water, and we'd put it in an orange. We'd take a hypodermic needle and we'd put it in the segments of the orange. And we'd--we'd keep these separate. One guy would have all of the amphetamines and one guy would have all the Nembutals. And they'd go through the ward and they'd give them, they just hand one on this side, one on the other side. And so we'd have half--half the side sleeping all day, and the other half couldn't sleep at all. They--they were--they'd be on the stay awake pills, they couldn't sleep. They'd say man, I don't know what's happening. All of them guys are sleeping and we can't--I can't sleep a bit. You know. So we did a lot of things we probably shouldn't have done. But we didn't really know anything about medicine, you know.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Are you still in touch with any of the people--any of your fellow--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Not--

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --people that you worked with at that time?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: No, not at that time, no. We had--we had--we had one man who came over, his name was Kasiah (ph). That was his real name. And we called him King Kong Kasiah. He was--he was--his head was shaved. And he was--he was a pretty mean looking guy to start with. And we'd take rubber bands and put them on his face and make like--looked like a big scar. And we'd use merthiolate to put and look like he was bleeding in places. And we'd use toothpaste to make his mouth foam, you know. And we passed the story around that--that Kasiah was a Navy chaplain who had gotten captured by the Japanese on Guadalcanal, and was tortured but escaped. And so if you wanted to see Kasiah, you had to make an appointment ____+ you had to have an appointment with either I or one of the other corpsmen. And there was one kid, his name was Kessler. And his dad was a psychiatrist in Washington, D.C. And this young man wanted to be--he wanted to see King Kong. I told him, I said, I don't think you're ready for that, I don't think you should see him. So he kept after me for about 10 days. So finally I said all right, you can come up there. And I called the ward and told them to get him ready, you know. So Kessler and I came up to the ward. And all the guys--all the patients knew what was going to happen, so they're all sitting up in their bunks. And the guys had King Kong in the utility room and they were getting him all ready. And pretty soon--and Kessler was sitting at a desk just reading a magazine. And when King Kong came up, why Kessler jumped right over the desk and he ran to the door. But the Marine guard would be on the other--on the other wall. Then by the time the Marine guard would get there to unlock the door, and King Kong would be too close to Kessler. So he would have to come back, and run the other way. And of course King Kong--this went on for about a half an hour. And finally--finally we--we had to stop it because I didn't know what was going to happen to Kessler. It was--I don't think he ever became a psychiatrist. Or anything.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Well, did you have any nicknames?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, I did. Later on I was called moose.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: But that was at the time I finally caught a ship. I was--I was--I was in the Navy and I wanted very bad to get overseas. I mean, to me, I mean, being--being in the states was worst thing that I thought could happen. So I was transferred from Philadelphia Navy Hospital to Bainbridge, Maryland, and I went through dental school, became a dental technician. Okay. When I went to dental school in--at Bainbridge, and my--the doctor that I worked with was Dr. Nelson, whose son is Don Nelson who coaches basketball. So sometimes when I see Don Nelson coaching a team, I think of him when he was very, very small. He was just a kid then and his dad was my dental instructor. He was a-- Dr. Nelson was a very good dentist. That would have been about the middle of 1943. I went from there then to Camp Lejeune, New River, North Carolina. And I was with the--I was with the marines at the--at the headquarters company there at Hadnot Point. I was doing teeth cleaning, teeth. You know. Prophylactic work on teeth. And I--I liked it all right. It was fun. We had some fun times there. The marine--the Navy--excuse me--the lady's basic was at Lejeune at that time. And I remember it was right after the marines had started taking the ladies into the service and they called them--Look Magazine had a big picture of them, called them beautiful American marines. And we changed that a little bit. So it wasn't beautiful American marines any more. And so when we'd see these--when we'd see these girls marching, we'd go--we'd say bam, bam, bam, you know. They'd become very, very mad. We'd say what do the big guns say, bam, bam, bam. They didn't like us very well. And I--I stayed there for about 4 months. Then I was transferred to--still in 43, I went to Norfolk, Virginia. And while I was in Norfolk, I worked for a place called NLFED, navel landing force equipment depot, where they re-corked the bottom of the Higgins craft, which are the--which are the vehicles that they land with, coming into the shores. And so while I was there, they didn't have any quarters for the corpsmen, for the medical people. We all had--we all stayed on in the--in motels and different places. Some guys in rooming houses, and so on. And so if you had the duty, you had to--you had to leave the number where they could reach you. So this one particular night, they--I had the duty and they called me and I went to--I went to the--I went to the--my duty station. And there they had brought a man in who was in a wicket stretcher. Big wire stretcher. And this man was from Iowa. And he had a very sore throat. But he was also stiff when he would move. Or when I have him roll his shoulders he was sore. And so we had to transfer him to the Portsmouth Naval Hospital. But to transfer him, we had to have a diagnosis undetermined. It was called DU diagnosis. So I thought well, I will transfer him with strep throat. But I thought, he's a little--it's a little more than that. So I looked up the big manual we had and I come across spinal meningitis. So I transferred him with spinal meningitis to the hospital at Portsmouth. And when we got to Portsmouth, we had to--we had to wash the ambulance down with alcohol because that was the diagnosis I had made. And the driver didn't like me very much after that. But anyway, we got back to--got back into the swing of things back at NLFED. And about a week later I got a call from the doctor in Portsmouth. And he told me to come down there right away, he had to see me. So I went down there and he was--he was a Navy captain. And he said to me, how much medical school have you had? And I said I haven't had any. I said, I haven't had any medical school at all. Well he said, that diagnosis you made on that patient was a hundred percent right. He did have spinal meningitis. And he said, if you hadn't made that diagnosis, we'd have had to--we'd have put him in an open ward and we'd have had to quarantine that whole ward. So he said, you did a real good deal by having the right diagnosis. I want to know how you came across that diagnosis. And I couldn't--just couldn't tell him I just looked it up. I--he asked me if I was interested in being--going to the V12 program and becoming a doctor. I think it's V12. It was either V12 or V6. And I said I would like to but, I said, I want to get overseas first. I came in the Navy to go and get into combat. I said I haven't been there yet. So he said then you're not interested? I said no, I'm not. So I went back to--to--to the NLFED. And while I was there I was getting into a lot of fist fights. And the fellow that I lived with, his name was Crandall, and he lived--he was from Two Rivers, Wisconsin. And he had been a corpsman on the Susan B. Anthony when it was sunk, a troop ship. And so one night--one night when neither one of us had duty and we're sitting in a bar. And we're talking about him being on the ship that was sunk. And I told him, I said, I sure hope I get an opportunity to, you know, to go through something like that before this is over with. Before the war is over with. And he said oh, he said, everybody says that. I said no, I said, I really mean it. He said, you do not. So we got into a big fist fight. And we had the same--we had the same doctor, same doctor who would also our commander. And so I went to this commander--both of us had to go to this commander and talk to him. Of course it was my fault and it was my second--second time that month that I had been there. And he said to me, he said, you're--you're in trouble a lot. Yeah, I said, I am. I said, I said, I joined the Navy to get into combat, and I said, I said, I said I haven't been able to get there. I said, all I've ever done is go from one duty station to another with nothing about combat. He said well, he said, if you really mean that, he said, I can have you ducking shell in 6 months. I said that's fine, that's what I want to do. So I was assigned to the U.S.S. Wisconsin. And the U.S.S. Wisconsin was at Philadelphia. So I went back to Philly where I had been before. And got assigned to the Wisconsin. That was really great. But by this time it was--it was probably April 1944. And I became ship's company of the Wisconsin. I didn't actually make the shake down crew. I wasn't the first people that had--the original crew--I was not with the original crew. But I--one of the men--one of the men had--had dropped out and he--so that I was a replacement for that crew. So I was a--my duties on the ship would be--I'd be--I was a dental technician. But because I had been a long time corpsman on sick hall at different--had many different patients, I spent more time in sick bay than I probably did in the dental offices. We had--we had three dental officers and four corpsmen. And I--and I would do a lot of stuff, both dental wise but a lot of stuff in the sick bay area too. Which I really liked a little better because ____+ I can do. By this time I'm still not liking being a medic, but--being a hospital man, but I'm learning to like it a little better. I was a pharmacy mate second class. Which would be about an E5 rating I think. And while we were in Philly, and we were going to move out, we were--ship was leaving Philadelphia. This particular morning, and I don't remember what morning it was, but when the sun came up, the man had hung himself on the yardarm, one of the crew members of the ship. And he had pinned a note on himself that said they expect so much from so few. And I never really did understand what he really meant. But it was quite a shocker for a lot of people. And I--I--I guess I don't know any more about that than that. We went out then and we went through the Cape Hatteras area and got in typical storm in Cape Hatteras, is always stormy there, and then through the Panama Canal. And we pulled liberty in Balboa as we went through the canal. And we went from there to the west coast, from the west coast to Pearl Harbor. And in Pearl Harbor--in Pearl Harbor then is where I got my nickname, Moose. And I got it because I was in some trouble there, too. The Navy come over looking for me and they said you mean that big moose of a guy? And they said that was me. So from then on I was Moose. But the shipmates and everything, everybody that I served with aboard the ship, very, very good people. We left Pearl Harbor and went on into the pacific area. And we got there about the time of the invasions of the Philippines. And we joined the third fleet under Admiral Halsey. And in the battle for--the Japanese were bringing many people in to re-invade the Philippines that we had already invaded. And I don't know what all the logistic things were on there. But I think--I think that we--I think we became kind of drifted away from the main body of things. I think the main invasion--the main sea action was done by ships other than the one I was on. And at that time I was third fleet, task force 34. Which was a fast carrier group. Everybody in the--all the units in there could maintain about 34, 35 knots. Really move. And so while we're out in this thing, we ended up in a--in a storm in the South China Sea, in December of 44. And I guess I should have said one thing before that. And that was when we got into the pacific area, there was a bunch of smoke coming down and you could see there was a ship being sunk. And the man I enlisted with in the Navy was aboard it. It was the U.S.S. Princeton. He went down with the ship. So that was my--that was my first day of seeing enemy action. But we see--we didn't do any action, it was action other ships had already done. And then we--we went in and we went into the--supporting the operations of the Philippines and we supported around there for awhile. And then I think there was--there was supposed to be some kind of a movement that we were going to make, and while we were making this movement we got caught in a typhoon. And this was a really serious typhoon that they said the winds were over 200 miles an hour. And the waves are like 150 feet high. And it was--it was a real disaster. We had--we had 3 ships that were sunk in that typhoon. They were the Hull, the Monaghan, and the Spence. And some of the crew that were saved off some of them, I think we lost about a total of 900 people on those three destroyers. And we had people being blown off other ships too. The U.S.S. Hancock had lost 80-foot of its flight deck, just crumbled it right up. It was real--really a bad--bad deal. And during this time--the first day of that typhoon, the man in the anchor windlass locker came out to put a tarp on a 20-millimeter that was up--way up on the ____. And before he could get back down to the anchor windlass locker, we--we must have went under and it--he ended up about 300 feet back. He was wrapped around a 40-millimeter quad. And he fell between the quad and the ammo box. So they had to--they had to get him off there. So three of us corpsmen went up there to get him off. I was the first guy out and they had tied a rope on me. And 20 feet behind me, or maybe 15, John Havanic, and then a guy named Jennings was the third guy. Then when I got out there, then I would pull the wire stretcher out and with three of us got this man off the--off--got him out of the situation he was in where his leg had been pinned in the--in between this--between the ammo box and the--and the round base of the 40-millimeter. And we--we put him in the basket and they pulled him in. And they got him inside. But before they got all of us in, I ended up--I ended up going down--out--I fell off the ship, or I was washed off. And I was washed off. But I had a hold of the foot line, the bottom line. And they had--they had a rope around me. So truthfully I was not really scared. I was uncomfortable, but I knew I was going to get back on it all right. And they did. They pulled real hard and they--I still--I can feel--for many years, I could feel a tightness here over my one kidney area. In fact, when I was in Korea I went to a hospital ship and then I--for that very reason. And they--they looked--they looked at it there. And--and then I told them what that was from. But anyway, that was a--that was--that was one day on that ship. We got the guy in the--into sick bay and they--they had--they had to amputate his leg. And--but he did live and he did make it. We transferred him then to a hospital ship. There were--on one of the ships that had gone down--we had just gotten the rubberized flashlights. They were kind of new then and everybody was supposed to have one. And I remember one time, when the storm was blowing out, and it was just about done, you could see a bunch of these people all in a cluster with these lights. I'm sure this was one of the ships had gone down and these guys are all still staying pretty close together. And they requested--they requested deviating from our course half a degree to miss these people. But because they were trying to get everybody back from all the ships in formation again, they couldn't do it. So we went right through these colonies. One colony. And I'm sure there were others that were there--of these people that were missing. Okay. When the storm finally did--did blow over, and all the ships got back in formations, and we did go back down to the Philippines and we--we--we're going through the San Bernardino straits, which is right south of the Philippines. And while we were in there, we were attacked by some--by the first kami--first Kamikaze planes that we heard of were there. And the--we had two destroyers, one was the Maddox and one was the McDermott. And the Kamikaze got one of them. The other one--the other one was hit real hard when the U.S.S. Missouri didn't get its guns up far enough and quick fired, fired too fast, and hit their ship. And we took the casualties from both the McDermott and the Maddox. The ships didn't sink, but had a lot of--too many casualties for them to handle. So they--I don't know exactly the number. But I think the number would have been close to 40 or 50 patients that we got. And they brought them--they brought them from the ship, from their ship to our ship. And part of the work I was doing was helping them unload, and load, and bring them back down to sick bay. And these guys--some of these guys were really badly shot up. And I remember after--after we got them unloaded, there was two ships, I remember both of them were the same. When they--as soon as they--as soon as they had the patients off there, well, the first thing you did was use big high pressure hoses to wash the decks on these destroyers. And I remember--I remember the--I remember the blood in water, looking just -- just like dego red wine. I mean, it was just--just that same color on both of those. It was just--it just struck me that I could remember that so plain. We went down, then there--we--I and John Havanic were working together, we were loading the casualties, off loading them from the destroyer and loading them on stretchers to go downstairs, down below decks. And while we were doing this, why, they were chow call and we were late for chow. But they said if you guys hurry, you know, you can make it. So we went, we were--we were real bloody. From top to bottom. And I mean, I--I mean, I--I never thought nothing of it. Neither did John. And we're down in the galley where we eat chow, and this guy--a couple other guys were eating late chow too. And they said what's the matter with you guys, are you guys--are you corpsman or what? John said yeah, we're unloading these patients. He said you mean that's blood? Yeah. They quit eating right there. They couldn't--they couldn't finish. So we ruined their appetite. Yeah. We--of these casualties, when they--when the Missouri quick fired, one round went over the splinter deck into the superstructure and the other one just below it and hit the steam room--the steam room. And three of the men were in the steam room. Two of them were wearing just the boxer shorts that the Navy had--skivvy shorts, and the third guy was wearing shorts plus cut off dungarees. Cut off like right here. And he was not burned quite as bad as the other two. But these guys were steam burned. And the guy that was--the guy that was--had the dungarees on, we could feed him to the vein in his penis and just left the needle there. But the other two--the other two were burned there too so we couldn't feed them there. And we got--it became my job to chew the food for these people and put it from their mouth--my mouth to theirs. I and another guy by the name of George Heath, both of us had to do this. It was a job I just thoroughly hated. I mean, I still hate it. I think--I think it was the worst thing I had to do. You know. And--but they did live. And they had to--there were other--other casualties there at the same time. They were--that I remember. I think we had 3 or 4 die right away. One kid--one young sailor, his name was Gilbert, he had--he had not a mark on him. And while he was waiting in the triage area, he died. And when they--and he stayed there that long in the triage area because--because he wasn't bleeding, or he wasn't--no visible signs of being hit. And so he--he died while he was waiting. And the doctors didn't understand why. And nobody else did either. So they X-rayed him. And a piece of shrapnel had caught under the base of his--of his hair line and got into his brain. Killed him that way. And I--I remember a sailor by the name of Tresh, who had a--who had a big eagle tattooed on his chest. He had other tattoos too. But this one big eagle was tattooed on his chest. And when he came--he was hit--he was hit so you couldn't have put a quarter on him without hitting two places. He was just plastered with shrapnel. And they took X-rays and then it just didn't hit anything vital. And when he--when he came out of it, why the first thing he said is did they ruin my tattoo? And I said yeah, I said, I think they did. Yeah, they did. Okay. These burn--these burn guys were really good patients and they--they made it. I just wish I would have kept--been able to kept track of who they were and where they were. But I didn't do that. We had--the other patients we had pretty much transferred them to hospital ships, to a destroyer and then to the hospital ship. But by this time we were getting pretty heavily into the Kamikaze part of the war. And we had--we were making--our next engagement was going to be the one on Iwo. And some of us got ashore on Iwo, but we went ashore there to triage patients, we weren't there as rifle team, corpsmen or anything. We were just there to--as ship's company and we did what we were supposed to do and came back to the ships. But the Kamikaze thing didn't really hit us hard until Okinawa, which was April 1, 1945. And at Okinawa, during that campaign, they--we were--we were under fire 5 and 6 times a day for 65 days. And I went from 185 pounds to 50--153. And I--I was in bad shape. I was sleeping with my eyes open. And I--this just--it just seemed like the Kamikaze thing was just getting to be too much. Not just for me, but for everybody else too. One of our--one of our commanders was on the phones that would radio throughout the ship, the events of these attacks. And they--they--he--and he lost it while he was on there. He just--he had planes diving from all angles after the thing was all over with. And they called from sick bay and asked me what was going on, and that's what was going on. And we transferred--got ahold of this commander and we took him down to sick bay and he was transferred to a hospital ship. So when they found out--when I found out I was sleeping with my eyes open. Because I didn't have any idea I was. But I heard--I heard one of the corpsmen Jennings talk to a Dr. Hogan. And he said, he said Moose is sleeping with his eyes open. He said it really makes me miserable when I'm up, he said, his eyes are looking at me. He said, scares the hell out of me. I said, I said, I don't believe that. I'm not sleeping with my eyes open. Dr. Hogan said well, horses do it all the time. And he said, he said men can if you're really stressed out. He said if you're really stressed out, that can happen. So I was pretty well stressed. And I--by this--by this time Okinawa was--was winding down. After the 65 days, it was pretty--it was pretty much over. And we--and we--we went down to Hokkaido and we did some bombardments on the north island of Japan, and then they dropped the bomb, and the war was pretty well finalized. But we--we--not just the Wisconsin but a lot of the heavy ships were designated as--as people--occupational forces, to make sure the people from--the occupational forces came from the Philippines and that they would be able to--that everything was on the up and up. The war would really be over. So we went in there, and we would--we'd see Japanese for the first time. And--and as a rule, everything went pretty well. But one time I was trying to buy a little watch or a fountain pen in this curio shop. And this Japanese was pulling all this stuff away. And so I went in the door to see him. And when I walked in the room he ran into another room and I followed him. I followed him into the next room. And into the third room. Then he pulled out a big--a big sword and he said you Yankee son of a bitch. And before he could start after me with that sword, I was back out on the street. I know he meant business. We also--we had a deal at--where MacArthur in Yokohama had his headquarters. And we had--we had people that were jumping off the wall there. And this one particular place this man jumped off the wall, and he had a brown pin striped suit on and was carrying a satchel. And when he did, he jumped just about on us three guys, I, John Havanic, and Jonnny--or Al, Al Cunningham. And when he did, we got the satchel from him. And in the satchel was a jeweled dagger and a nazi cigarette case, and a bunch of papers that we couldn't read so we just left them, and then a watch and watch fob and chain. That was--that was about the only souvenirs we got out of the whole--the whole thing. From there we--from there we went back home. The war was over. We went through the Golden Gate Bridge. And then the first day--the first day at Hunters Point where we landed in Frisco, the one man who had been burned the least, from the--steam burned the least, came out to see us, said the other two were doing fine too. So that was pretty much it. Okay, that picture was taken after the war, and after we come back after--after the war. This is a picture of us after we graduated from basic training. See it's December the 10, 1942. Yeah, that would be a picture of me with the group that graduated in 10 December of 1942. Okay, this is a--this picture of the Wisconsin, and this is--this is where this man I mentioned is going to put the tarp on a 20-millimeter up at the ____ hull. And it carried him all the way back to about this part. ____ it would have been on the starboard side. And wedged in between a 40-millimeter mount and the ammo box. That would be almost--almost--be a long ways. Almost half way. Okay, I got discharged then in February of--of 1946. And that was one of the toughest days I think I ever had was leaving the ship. That's the day I--I just--I just--I really would have liked to have stayed. And I had an offer to stay. I could have gotten an E7 if I'd have stayed. But I didn't know how it would be back home. I didn't want to leave my folks short on help again. My other two brothers were still in the service 'cause I went in before they did, I got out before they did. And when I got home, I had a--I had a hard time. I was--it seemed to me like the war was not over yet then. It just seemed to me like--like things were happening so fast, I couldn't--I just couldn't comprehend them. I and my dad were walking down the street in Crookston, which is a bigger town, and was in--it was probably in March. And the spring thaw. And somebody honked a horn and I dove in the gutter. You know, just--I mean, I was so jumpy, I was so hyper alert, any noises or anything that would bring me back to those--those Kamikaze days. And I had a hard time with it. Very, very hard time. I would be out in the--I'd sometimes find myself out in the cattle yard at 20 below with no clothes on hollering at my folks to come out and get me. And they never could understand what was the matter with me. They--I guess they thought I was really bad. When I--I started having trouble on the ship during--during these Kamikaze days, and I lost a lot of weight and I was sleeping with my eyes open. But I started coming down with hives, gigantic hives, really, really bad. And so I asked the doctors if they were going to send me to a hospital ship. And they said no, they wouldn't, because they thought if I ended up in an insane asylum, I'd never get out of there. So instead they wrote a letter to my folks and to some of the other people I knew, the minister and my dad's friends, not to talk about the war with me. And I think that was harder on me than anything. Because I would probably start a conversation with somebody and they'd--they'd turn it off right away. That's--I had trouble with that--I doctored with those hives for 40 some years. It just--it just finally, finally, finally in Minneapolis I was able to get some help. But it took many, many, many years.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Glenn, it's been a real honor getting to know you. And I really respect you and admire you for what you have done for so many people. And that we appreciate everything that you have given us in our lives. The second taping that you're going to do will tell about your continued experience where you went on and were involved with the Korean War, which took tremendous strength. And you mean a lot to this country and we want you to know that you're honored. And thank you for being part of the veterans history project. And this will be continued on another tape. And thank you very, very much.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: You're very, very welcome. It was an honor for me to do it. * * * * * *

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: My name is Kristen Miller. Today is July 31, 2002. We're at the Colmery-O'Neil VA Medical Center in Topeka, Kansas. Today we have the honor and privilege of interviewing Mr. Glenn Ray Sheridan. Mr. Sheridan resides at 1242 Southwest Western, in Topeka, Kansas, 66604. Mr. Sheridan was born in Neilsville, Minnesota on September the 4th, 1925. It's an honor because Mr. Sheridan served both in World War II and the Korean War. We have filmed a history presentation of World War II from Mr. Sheridan, and now we are continuing with his experience in the Korean War. His dates of service were March 22, 1951, through March 25, 1955. Again, we're privileged and honored to interview him for his Korean War experience. I know from our World War II interview that it is okay to call you Glenn. Is it still okay?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Sure is.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: You served in World War II, and then you made a decision again to re-enlist and fight over in Korea. Can you tell us how that decision was made?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, it was made on the day that the North Korean troops invaded the south. I knew as a Navy corpsman, that I would be able to go over there and be of some help. The Marine Corps does not have any medical personnel, they get them from the Navy. And by the time--at the end of World War II I was pretty confident that I had--could handle most casualties. So when Korea started, I just--it was just something come over me that I had to go.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: What was your situation at that time--

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I was--

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: --since World War II?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I was married then, and I had two children. Was running country grain elevators. And so I couldn't get away right away. In fact--in fact the harvest was coming in in Minnesota, and--living in northern Minnesota, and running grain elevators, and the harvest was coming in. So I was not able to check out of the elevator until March. But as soon as I could, I joined--I joined up. My ex-wife didn't want me to join up. She was--she didn't want me to leave there because--because I was making more money running grain elevators, naturally. So she had went down to the recruiter and told the recruiter not to enlist me. But I--I--I went to this recruiter and the recruiter was very honest with me. He said my wife had been there, told him not to enlist me. But he had written to DC and gotten my records and said I had a good record in World War II, and if I wanted to come back in, he wouldn't stand in my way. When I got discharged from World War II, I was a second class pharmacist mate. And the--the rating had been changed then to hospital man. But it was second class. And I was a dental technician in World War II. So I told the recruiter that I would come in but I wanted to be broke down to a third class hospital man and not be a dental tech, because I wanted to be sure I got with the line troops. Had I stayed second class, I would have been battalion aid or medical battalion. But as third class and below, I would be in with a line company, which is what I wanted to be. So that's--that's how I decided I wanted to go to Korea. I went--my duty--my first duty station was Philadelphia. And when I got to Philadelphia, I was at the Navy yard, and some of the work we were doing was drawing blood from people for just various tests. And we were drawing on civil work--civil service workers, civilian people. And I had one particular person who I was not able to get the--hit the vein on very well and so I asked the chief to take me off that and let somebody else do it. But he said no, you stay with it. And so I did. The party that I was drawing blood from was pretty upset with me, but I did--I did stay and I finally got it at--on their ankle. But I was--I found out later that it--the chief was doing me the right thing by making me do this, because in Korea I had to do this. I had to find the vein that--some people which were losing blood fast, you had to be able to get the ____ and real quick. So it all had a reason. But when I got to Philadelphia to Navy Hospital, I asked right away to be transferred to the fleet marine force at Camp Pendleton, California. And they said--the man there said no, he said, you were in World War II, and we have a lot of people that weren't in World War II, so he said, they're all going to go to Korea first. He said you won't go until they come back. I said how long will that be? He said probably two to 3 years. So I said well, I joined to get to go to Korea. He said well, he said, I'm sorry, but we're not going to send you there. So I was fortunate in being able to trade orders with a man who was going to Bainbridge, Maryland. Well, he and I were both hospital men third class and his family was living in Philadelphia, so he stayed there and I went to Bainbridge, Maryland. And the day that I got there, I requested captain's mass and seen the skipper and applied immediately for FMF duty. And he granted it to me. He sent me. So I got to Camp Pendleton and started fleet marine force training. They have quite a--they had a pretty extensive field training course, to get you adapted to the Marine Corps ways. So I--I--I enjoyed the training because I was looking forward to going to Korea with them. And--but because of World War II, I was real subject to noises. And I--I would--I would--I was real hyper alert. And so on the day that we went through the live fire course, it was a two section course, with a--with a trench in the middle. And I--and they assign you a lane. And they knew I think I was pretty jumpy, so they assigned me to this lane that had a lot of the explosions. So by the time I got to the second trench, I was not so sure I wanted to keep going. But there was a captain there and three sergeants, and they just picked me up and threw me into the other lane so I had to keep going. And I'm awful glad they did, because otherwise I may have--I may have decided I couldn't make it. But because of that, I could make it. So I--I ended up going to Korea on the 13th replacement draft. And we left--we left the states in September of 51 and got to Korea in October of 51. I got assigned to the--to a company in November, and I got assigned to Charlie Company first engineer battalion. And I questioned that because I thought well, I'd rather be with a rifle company. But they said because of my World War II experience aboard ship, I had taken care of a lot of casualties from explosions and--and bullets, Kamikaze type thing, and they thought that would be some of the same type casualties we would have in Korea. So I was assigned to Charlie Company. And we would go on--on mine details right away. And because it was frozen--excuse me--it was--the weather there was pretty cold and it was frozen, and a lot of snow, a lot of times we'd be out with the--with the element of the company that did road work and grading work. And so one time we were out with a mine detail and they had a--they had a bulldozer working there too. And the bulldozer was cutting a grade by a little river. This is on Hill 812. And--and all of a sudden mortar started coming in. The first two--first one come in I'm sure was a dud, but these kids got quite a kick out of myself and one of the senior sergeants hitting the deck right away because nothing happened. But just like that, then, the rounds came in. They were walking them in in groups of fours. And this was on December 21, 1951. And the first round that come in hit a guy on the dozer. So he immediately called for a corpsmen, and then that was me that had to go up there with him. But I couldn't come down the road because they were walking these mortars down the road, so I cut off by the mountains and went through a mine field, and then cut back to the road. And as I did, they would walk these mortars in, in four. I could hear them coming, and as soon as I thought they were coming in close, I would hit the deck. And I made it all the way to the road without--without any injuries. When I got to the road, I just got to the road and I was going down after this guy on the dozer. And a round come in and I--and I dove into the ground. And I remember the--I didn't get hit with any shrapnel but the--but the concussion--concussion knocked me pretty silly for awhile. I remember--I remember putting my left knee back in--back in. I had dislocated my knee, or so I thought, and I put my knee back in. And I had just getting up and I--there was a--as I remember it, and I think I was delusional, but there was a--I seen an army lieutenant, and his army was in the brown uniform, and he had a potato masher grenade, and he's saying what should I do with it? I'd tell him throw it in the river. And he didn't, but I grabbed it and I threw it in the river and put it in the river. And so anyway, I was the only person who seen this lieutenant so I know that I was probably out of my head. I ran up then--or I should say I limped up to where the dozer was and the--the guy was not hit very hard. But they were evacuating him. Our trucks were there anyway evacuating him. They asked if I wanted to go be evacuated. And I said no, I didn't, I wanted to be with the main party. So I went back to the main group and we went across. So when I got back with the main group, then we went across the river and over another mountain and--a low one this time. And then there were trucks waiting to evacuate us. As we got there there was a big rock pile and the mortars kept coming in. And I got behind some rock pile part thing and I got screened from the shrapnel again. But I--I was able to see the arc of the mortar with my right eye and it was like a welding arc. To this day I have a real lot of trouble with light on the right side of my--of my face. I also--I also lost my sense of smell that day. You could just feel the air coming back up and I suppose that's when I lost it. I haven't been able to smell since. Anyway--anyway, I went back and--we went back to the company and then they asked me then to--to go to the--to the med battalion and I--I think I was still out of it a little bit because I thought, well, I'd be okay, you know, my knee will be okay. I didn't want to take a chance of leaving the bunch, I wanted to stay here because I'd figured I'd spent too much time trying to get here. So I wanted to stay. But anyway, I--I stayed with the bunch. And about three days later, I had to go in because my knee was getting worse. So I--I--when I went back in then I just went in for line of duty, so I made myself out of the purple heart. But that was all right. But anyway, while we were in there that winter, it got pretty cold. I've seen where they--where they talked about it going down to 40, 41, 45 below for us that year. And we lived in bunkers because we were part of the line. We were tied up with--had marines on our left flank and KMCs on the right side. The KMCs is ____ marines. And we--we lived in the bunker. There was probably about 6 or 7 of us per bunker. And the North Koreans were real great about coming in at night and harassing you. They come in and they fire what's called H and I, harass with intent. And so we--we'd have our guns up and firing back. And I never could understand why we have to go out and police the brass when we got done. As soon as--as soon as the firing mission was over, they'd say all right police all the brass. I thought boy, this is silly. So I asked one of the sergeants one day and he said, well, he said I'll tell you what, you come out with me early in the morning and I'll show you. So I did, and--and when the sun come up, why the sun shined real bright on the brass that we were--our guns were throwing out and now I can see they knew where each heavy position was, where all our automatic weapons were. That's what they were trying to do with this H and I firing. But we lived--we lived in bunkers and we had one warm up tent. And in this one warm up tent we had--it was a--it was just out behind our bunkers and you could go there and you could shave and have warm water, it was a helmet type thing. But while I was there, they knocked that tent down three times with mortar fire. They come in--it just seemed like they had a route, had a tube right on it because they--so they didn't hit very many people in there. Well, we were in this--in this area. We would go out on a lot of--the patrols that we would go out on, we would go out in the mountains, the snow would be like 12-foot deep in some of these cuts. So we'd go out on the same path all the time and the North Koreans would be coming back on the same path every time, and we'd meet each other sometimes. I know once or twice we had fire fights where I know we didn't have any casualties and I'm sure they didn't either. But it would be movement to contact type patrols. We'd just go out until we'd make contact and then we'd come back. So that's pretty much what we did all that winter. We had--stayed--as far as staying warm in those bunkers, we had no heat. But we had--we had arctic sleeping bags and we found out if you--if you--if you took most of your clothes off, in the arctic bag, you could stay pretty warm. If you slept in them with a lot of clothes on--but quite a challenge because you didn't have any light and--and of course we lived on sea rations so we--we lived in there, we ate there and everything else. It was pretty much--pretty much self contained. Even though it was very cold out, we stayed pretty warm because our winter gear was--was pretty good. We had--we had vapor barrier boots and--and--and we didn't have too much trouble with--with that sort of thing. One time while we were up there, some inspector came by and asked when they had last had a hot meal. And of course, it had been a long time. So he--he said--so he said he was going to take care of that. They sent a couple trucks up, and one was a kitchen truck and they fried eggs, and we had our mess kit. And--and it was 21 below that morning and so we'd get--we'd get the fried eggs and they would freeze before you could find a place to sit down and eat them. So everybody would just throw the whole mess kit, eggs and everything away. We went back and ate sea rations again. But the--the equipment we had was--was, I thought, really good for the weather we were in.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Had there been some improvements made?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Yes. Yes. The winter before, the frozen chosen ones, the ones that were over there--the frozen chosen bunch is December--November and December of 50. The year before. They--they--they were wearing shoe packs. And the shoe packs would get wet and they weren't able to--they weren't able to dry them out. And many of those guys had frost bitten feet. And they--they suffered a lot more. Plus the fact they were farther north. And I think the temperature was colder than it was where we were. Temperature where we were was very cold too. We had one incident where--where a--where there was a mess--they built a mess hall up on the line. And I know they--they told us not to be near that mess hall. Our gunny sergeant said don't be near that mess hall because, he said, that's the foolish thing they ever did. You put this hot mess hall--this mess hall up. And one day, the North Koreans put three rounds in that mess hall and they killed 43 guys and wounded about a hundred and some. So they had--so they had helicopters come up and haul these casualties out. The Marine Corps was using the little--little pod things, those little--little bell type helicopter with a plastic bell on it and the two pods. Is what the Marine Corps used. But the Army come and helped us out with some of their bigger ones. While we were there, my gunny sergeant got a call that--that there were--that this one helicopter had gone down. That they shot one of these small marine helicopters down with close arms fire. He got up the-- domed on the wrong canyon. And so they had him staked out, they had taken all his clothes off and they had him staked out. And the--the marines that were in front of him were going to jump off, try to get him back. But there were--there were--there were things out in front that they thought were probably mines, so they wanted--they wanted an engineer officer to come up and look. So the sergeant went up there and I went up with the sergeant, he asked me to go with him. So I went with him and we were standing up on the parapet looking at this--where these were. And I--and I think the sergeant said really what they are is probably a bunch of batteries that are--that had thawed one time and some of them were sticking out of the snow. And anyway, all of a sudden we got--we got fired on. And--and the rounds went over me. And they went over the sergeant I was with. But the infantry sergeant showing us where the--where this man was staked out, he got hit in the shoulder. So I went down the parapet, and had my weapon with me. And when I did I seen who was firing, it was a man in a spider trap. And he was firing--he was firing at us. I think he--I think he thought he got us. Got me and the sergeant I was with. Because he looked up then again to fire up in there and of course nobody was up there. Because everybody was down. But I had a shot at him and I took it. And I was able to--I was able to shoot him out of the spider trap. And we went back then to our units, and I don't think they ever did jump off. To get this--I heard that they had jump off and they had set a--the North Koreans had set up a double cross fire, with machine guns, two on each side. And they finally did get this man but it took a whole lot of infantry to get him. One other--one other incident I remember in Korea was the--we were out on a--on a--we were working--the marines were working on a bridge--on a bridge deal. I think they were putting up a Bailey bridge. And there was a bunch of cable and stuff. And all of a sudden planes came and strafed us, four planes came over and strafed us. And we'd seen these planes, they were our own planes, they were all their own markings and everything. And then they came back up, and they formed up and they came back the second time. When they came back the second time, I was on the ____ slope, in a slope, so when they would make their run, they came down and they were--they were real low and they were firing in there again. At people at the bridge. And I--and I fired up at the--at the guy at the lead plane. And anyway, they--they did--they still strafed and then they left. And then we found out right away they were planes from the U.S.S. Randova. And they apologized for, you know, for this incident happening. And what had happened was they--they had--they were having a regimental commander, new regimental commander, and they built a log type house for him out of wood up there. And the excuse was when these planes seen that they thought it was a permanent installation and they thought--we thought they thought we were North Koreans so they strafed us. And we--we didn't have any panel markers out, so it was kind of our fault too. But anyway--anyway, I got called in on that because I fired up at that plane. Oh, yeah. The guys on the Randova said one plane didn't make it back. And I got kidded then because I was firing up. But then there was some marines firing up too. But they called--they called me in there and they asked me why I fired at that plane when I clearly could see it was an American plane. And I said well, I been out in the pacific in the Kamikaze war. And I said--I said I was--I said I was a corpsman then too and I didn't have a weapon to fire back at anything. And I--and I felt like I had been a target all the way through. And when these guys started strafing, I got the same feeling again. So the--so the--my company commander said well, he said, that's understandable. So I didn't hear from anybody else. Okay, yeah. The--after--I got a couple pats on the back for shooting this guy out of the spider trap, that gave him--the day or two before that. But they said that--I mean, to me it made me feel, not good about killing this man, but it made me feel good that I had a weapon I could fire back with. Because all through World War II I was--felt more like a target because of the Kamikaze planes and everything, I had nothing at all for me to fire back with. The incidents--the--the living up in that part of Korea was a lot more severe. We changed coasts sometime in March of that year. And I also changed companies. I was--I was--went from Charlie Company to Dog Company. And in Dog Company I ran into a gunny sergeant was a man whom I'd known in the states before. His name was Powers. And he was--he was a really, really good man. He had the Navy Cross from Iwo Jima and he was--he just had the feeling for this kind of thing. And when we got to the west coast, there were no more mountains and the weather was much nicer, and the hills were much lower. I think--I think the big hill--we were on Bunker Hill, I think it was only 216 meters. And on the other side they were up to 1050 something. So they were much, much higher there. But we had a lot more mine--mine work in western Korea. Because the ground wasn't frozen as much, mine field. And different--different mine incidents I was on. One--I was on one with--with--with--we were supporting the first regiment, I don't remember what battalion. But we went out--we went out and--and we cleared a mine belt. Lieutenant by the name of Murphy and a then new lieutenant. Murphy was rotating back out, and there was a new lieutenant just coming in. And--and Lieutenant Murphy said I wonder if we cleaned that belt up over here. So he--so Lieutenant Murphy, Sergeant Crane, and a PFC named Hicks went up to check it out. And when they got up there, they got ambushed by Chinese. We had Chinese on this coast, and North Koreans on the other coast. So the Chinese ambushed these people, and we could hear the ambush. And as we moved to go around to--to ambush the ambush, to get around to get in back of them, then--then we were getting bracketed by the mortar fire. They bracketed, hit behind us and ahead of us, and then would lift it every so often and we'd move, so we'd move back up to the line. So anyway--anyway, that--the--when they--when they done this, Hicks--Hicks came back through--Private Hicks came back through the bracket. And he seen us, and I took care of him. He had--we had mine--we had bullet proof vests on by then, and he had hit--was hit nine times across here with a--with a--I'm sure, that was enough to knock him out, but it was just black and blue marks because the vest wouldn't penetrate. But when he was down, then they broke his upper law and his nose with a butt stroke of a rifle. And so he was a pretty bloody mess. Then he walked through that bracketed mortar fire and both his legs were hit. So I gave him first aid, and he stayed with us then until we got to the line. When we got to the line, then the infantry company jumped off, jumped back off here, to see if we could get these Chinese ambushed. So I went back with them. And when we did, we found Sergeant Crane, he was--he was--he was--they had taken his--all his clothes, and he was dead. And we blood trailed Murphy. They captured Murphy, and we trailed him with, you know, with blood droppings and things. As far as we could. Until it got too late, we had to come back. So we never--we never found out much about Murphy until after--afterwards, he was a prisoner of war. And so anyway, they--we were very disappointed they'd called in--set the bracket up. And so they--they were having a big discussion on it. And this new lieutenant was saying--he said I didn't call that bracket in. He said, the RTO called it in. That's the radio telephone operator. So I called--I called--I went and talked to the RTO and the RTO said no, he said, he said I wouldn't call that in. He said the battalion called it in. So I went back and I told this lieutenant, I said, you're lying. I said so and so didn't call it in. And we got into kind of a pushing match. And so anyway, this--my sergeant said, Glenn, you shouldn't have done this, you know, he said, this be the end of you here, you know, you can't do that. So I figured I would be transferred out. But the next morning, the jeep came up and this new lieutenant was being transferred out. So I said to Sergeant Powers, what happened? And he said well, he said, it's--it's a lot harder to get a good corpsman than it is to get a lieutenant. So I got by with that one. We--and we had other patrols. And this Sergeant Powers was in my book the best marine I ever seen. He--we once in a while would get dropped off on the wrong coordinates and we'd be on coordinates that we shouldn't be on and we'd have to find another way. And one time we were walking through this Chinese village, and you could just see these Chinese had taken all the Koreans out of it and they were in this village, and you could see their weapons pointing out at you. And I remember Sergeant Powers saying now don't look to either side, just look straight ahead, and don't make any moves for your weapons, just keeping walking. And we walked right through the village and nobody fired a shot and they never fired at us either. So I asked Sergeant Powers how can that be? He said well, he said, we were a small group, they thought we were an advance group for a bigger party. So they were waiting for the bigger ones. But if we had made any moves for them, why, they would have--they would have gunned us down. Then later on one time we were in a--we were in a vehicle then. And we were going through this village, and that's the way we were--thought we were supposed to be. I think the driver was lost. Anyway, we ended up in a Chinese held village too, and we were just about through it when they realized it was wrong. We'd seen these--these Chinese, and they were wearing kind of a black flowing uniform then. And so this guy turned around, we went out there, they shot at us the whole way out but we made it out okay. Thanks to Sergeant Powers. I mean, he--a lot of us would have been hurt. I mean, a good sergeant is worth a lot up there. So we--well, we--on different mine patrols, why, we would--we worked on--we'd work on these belts and we'd probably work on the same belt for, you know, like maybe--maybe up to two weeks. And when we would be out on some of these--some of these places, we would--we would be driven out to where the belts were, where the mine fields were. And then if it was at the wrong coordinates we'd be somewhere else. So this particular time we were out there and we were in the wrong spot. And a truck came by and it was a recon outfit. And so Sergeant Powers knew most of these guys. So he knew some of the guys in recon and they stopped and they told him where--Pinky knew where we were supposed to be. So they said okay that's fine, we'll bring you there, but first we're supposed to pick up--we got to pick up a prisoner, for interrogation. So this was in the same--same village that we had driven almost through again. So--so they said okay, you guys can wait here by this building, there was a little out building by there. And then when--and the recon people were going to decide how they would--how they would set that up. And as they were doing this, there was--there was--there was a young Chinese and--apparently in the building, and he came out of the building, and I suppose he'd heard the noise, and was walking along the outside of the building, on the end of it, and I was sitting closest to him. I didn't realize that, but I was the one closest to him. And so they started motioning me with--the recon people, you know, so then I realized what was happening. So I waited until he was just up there and I reached out and I grabbed him, you know, and I grabbed him, I pulled him back. And he couldn't have weighed more than 50, 60 pounds, he was real small. And of course the recon people grabbed him as soon as I--as soon as I brought him over to where they were. And so he was sitting there being interrogated. And--and he just couldn't take his eyes off me. He would be watching me out of the corner of his eye all the time. I suppose he thought I was--you know, I was the guy that got him and I suppose he was really mad at me, you know. Anyway--anyway, this incident kind of--I really kind of had forgotten pretty much about it. And I and my wife were at St. Louis for a Korean War reunion. And there was--it was at the same time that they were having a--an Olympic, I forget which one, but one of the Olympics, and they were showing the gymnasts of this Olympics. The girls had had their--they had theirs one day and the next day was going to be the men. So they panned in on these guys with the camera, and they showed this one Chinese fellow who was looking at everybody out of the corner of his eye. And it just took me right back to Korea. Just--just exactly like--like what I remember this Chinese prisoner. And so--and I just--it just really--it really affected me for the rest of the reunion. But it was about over with anyway. We'd driven up. So we drove back here and I--I -- Jackie had to drive just about the whole way because I was really--I was really shook. And so we stopped--so Jackie--Jackie said we'll stop, we'll go out to the hospital. It was Sunday. I said well, nobody's there. No, she said, we'll just drive around. And just driving around was enough to settle me back down again. But it was just something that flashed when I seen that Olympics. Then on--on another--another time we were out and we were working on--working on one of the belts and we got dropped on the wrong coordinates. So we walked this time. And we walked--when we'd walk, we'd walk single file. And--and I was a corpsman, I, you know, I carried special gear, so they could tell real quick who the corpsman was. So we--I didn't walk on the end, because it was--then they could identify you easier, so I'd walk in the middle. And this particular time I was walking behind a young man by the name of Duane Okey. And Duane was a football player from Illinois. Big rough kid. And all of a sudden he turned around and he smacked me right in the jaw and he knocked me down. And then he said doc, he said, I'm really, really sorry, he said, but he said, you were--you were--you were grabbing a wire. I was pulling a wire and I didn't--didn't know it. But Duane seen it out of the corner of his eye, seen the grass move, so he knew I had--I was dragging a wire. So I was dragging a wire and so I asked Pinky, I said, can I take care of this one? And he said well, he said, if you think you can, go ahead. His idea was that if the corpsman--if you were a corpsman and you were in a mine field, you should know a little bit about mines--about mines to pull your way out. The trouble with a mine field is you get hit in the mine field, it's almost impossible to get them out. They're devised so going to hit a wire one way or another. To I went up there and I was able--I probed underneath it just the way I was supposed to and hold the--pulled the pin out just the way I was supposed to. And then to put the other pin in, I dropped it. So I--so I didn't have the pin. But I had my first aid kit so I put a safety pin in it. So I put the safety pin in. From then on we put safety pins in all of our mines. And one time I and--I and my wife were at a--at an Iwo Jima reunion. And at Camp Pendleton they had--they had everything set up with--they had everything with an artillery display, and then an engineer display. And the young engineer that I talked to on his hat had 22 pins stuck in the crown of his hat. And I said why--why do you have them? He said that's for mines. He said ____ he said they stay in there better than the cotter keys do. So I knew where he got that idea. Yeah. We had--we had--we had one mine belt out in western Korea, it was just north of Panmonyeong (ph). And it was--it was actually in an area that was later to become Bunker Hill. And this--this belt was pretty big. We'd worked on it for over two weeks. And this--and we had--had not too many accidents out there. They had been going pretty well. And one--one day we came out there, they were hauling us out there, and Pinky noticed right away, had the truck stopped, because he noticed there was some--that somebody had been digging in the ground. And sure enough the Chinese had put a bunch of anti-tank mines right in the driveway where this truck would have taken us.
