So he--we unloaded there and he sent--he sent all of us but a guy -- a PFC named Rouch. Rouch and Pinky stayed to work on the anti-tank mines. So the rest of us--the rest of us went back to the main line, main belt that we had been working on all the while. And when we got--when we--just when we got there, we were about a quarter mile away, and heard a mine go, and then--and then three fast rounds with a 45. And so I knew right away that they were in trouble up there. So I grabbed my stuff and I started running. And this Okey started running when I did and he--and he would pass me and he'd--I'd give him the unit one, the first aid kit, and he would carry it until it would slow him down enough to where I could pass him, and we did that all the way up the hill. It was about 6--about a quarter of a mile. And when I got there, Sergeant Powers was--they were both--they were both hit. And what had happened was they had pulled an anti-tank mine off that was booby trapped with a shape charge. And they used the shape charge because if they were to hit a tank, the anti-tank mine would have blown off a track and then the shape charge would have blown through the--through the tank and killed the crew. But when--when they ____ when they pulled it, they just lifted this thing out, they didn't pull it. They didn't pull it really the right way. They were supposed to pull it with wire ____+ just away. But he--they lifted it out, they were careless, they wanted to get through it fast. And when it blew, it blew the side of Pinky's face off. It blew his nose off, and it blew his eye out, his ear off, and his teeth all were blown through his check. And his tongue was cut just about in half. And when I got there I could see right away he did'nt--I mean, he didn't have no face. He was laying there and I--and I got--I went to Pinky first, and I said I got you Pink. And I could just see him recognize him by making a motion with his hand. Sort of relax. And so I--I started working on--on Pinky. And Rouch was hit on the other side of the face. I thought he had lost an eye too. But I think they saved his eye. But he--at the time it looked like he had lost his. But he wasn't hurt near as bad as Pinky was. So as soon as I got to Pinky, I could see he was losing blood real fast. And I tried to put some pressure bandages on. But when I would lay him--his body was laying in, when I turn him over he had--into shock position or something, why then--then of course he would bleed more. So I gave him ____ right away, and I was able to hit his vein right away, and thank, you know, for that because whatever collapsing as he was losing blood. The vein collapses behind it. So I got--I got ____ in him. And then when Duane was putting a weapon in so I could use it to hang the blood bag on, then that blood bag was too high. The M1 was too long. And it was--flooded the needle, the vein wasn't taking it in as fast. So he had to put a carbine there. I carried a carbine as a corpsman. And that was just--that fed just right. But both times he hit other mines when he was putting these--he was hitting--they were all anti-tank mines, so it takes 250 pounds to detonate them. So we weren't in danger that way, we could walk out. But anyway, on Pinky, on--okay. So on taking care of Pinky that I knew I had to stop the bleeding, and yet he was strangling in his own blood. He couldn't breathe. You know. His nose was gone and his--and his tongue was almost torn away. So I did a tracheotomy on him. I cut a trach. I had a scripto pencil and I broke the end off the pencil and had to use the tube, and used that as an airway tube. And used a bunch of tape and taped it in. And then I took--I took some gauze and--off an inch roll and fluffed it up and put it in his mouth so it would absorb the blood there. Keep the bleeding down there. And I used compression bandages on his face. And pretty much--pretty much the same with Rouch. We pretty well could stop his with the compression bandages. They called in a helicopter, and one of these little bubble tops came in. And the pilot came right on down just about--just about on the ground but he wouldn't come in the ground because he knew it was a mine field. So he asked if the mines had been cleared, and they had not been cleared. So he said okay, he said, I want three guys on each side to kneel down on one leg, and then he put the helicopter right on their knee, on their other leg. And we put these guys on and they took them to Able Med. When they got to Able Med, the--they unloaded them from the helicopter and they put Pinky in the dead pile, they thought he was dead. But a friend of mine by the name of Ben Wolfe, who I--who I still talk to once in a while, knew both I and Pinky from Camp Pendleton. And he--he seen my signature on the--on the emergency medical tag and so he looked--he looked to see if it was Pinky and it--and he seen Pinky's name on it. So he--he said--he said, he said I just caught a little bit of movement. So he said, I told--I come in and told the doctor that guy's alive yet. So they--they took him in and flew him right out to a hospital ship or I think then from there right to Japan and then ____ California. And then they rebuilt his face there. So he did make it. You know, he--on Christmas of 1953--I got back to the states in--on Christmas--on the 21 of December of 1952. And--and I was--I was stationed at Camp Pendleton in the--with the third division. And they were retraining. And they were retraining. And I asked them what for, and they said they were retraining for a place called Vietnam. They couldn't go then. But right--they went later but they couldn't go then. But anyway, I was there during Christmas of 53 and I got word that Pinky was coming--was coming down. So I met him at the NCO club. And I thought he looked great. But the part of his face that was natural, as we were in the NCO club, would get redder than the other was. Pinky was from Glasgow, Montana and he had been a miner in the mines, so he was a demolition man, he--he knew his stuff good. And he--I thought he did fine. He had--had gotten a lung shot out on Iwo Jima and he was on a hundred percent disability, but he wanted to get to Korea. And he wrote a letter to Laman Sheppard (ph), who was a commandant in the Marine Corps, and because he had the Navy Cross they put him on active duty. I'm sure they didn't mean for him to go to Korea again, but he did go to Korea again. But this time they discharged him. So he was discharged, and he--he was very bitter about this. I didn't see Pinky any more then. The last time I seen him was on Christmas of 53. But I would keep track of--I would keep track of him through recruiters who said that they would--they had seen--I'd ask them if they'd seen gunny Sergeant Powers with a glass eye, and they said there was a man there at Pendleton with a glass eye, and I just took for granted that was Pinky. But it wasn't. So when I found out that it wasn't, I wrote to the Marine Corps magazine and asked if anybody knew what happened to Pinky Powers. He had shot himself ten years after--after the date of when he was--he committed suicide. And I really--I really felt bad. Really, really bad that I hadn't checked up on him, you know. I--I had gone to Glascow, Montana and I had tried to find--to find out--to find out more about him. I didn't really know his name. I knew it as Powers and everybody called him Pinky Powers because he was--he was pretty ruddy complected. But--so at one of the reunions, then, I was telling this story, and one of the guys said well, he said, I can find out his name. He was a historian for the fifth marines. And he--he said if he's got the Navy Cross, I can tell you what his name is. His name was James Joseph Powers. So then I went to--I found his headstone at the Rosecrans Cemetery in San Diego, the military cemetery there. So then I stayed with the third division for awhile, but my knee was pretty weak, so I--so I--they finally transferred me to do duty at the Corona Navel Hospital. And while I was at the Corona Navel Hospital my enlistment ran up. And--and they wouldn't re-enlist me because of my knee. And I had--I didn't have a knee--a history on my knee because--and I don't really know why, because I had been in the--in the Able Med with it. But the med station had burned down shortly after I was there and I think part of my records did too. And I have tried since to establish some connection but I'm not able to establish a connection. So I--I have--I have an injury from playing football on the knee, but that's--but I don't have one for being--for the day in December of 51. But I--the Navy would not re-enlist me because of my knee. They would--I shouldn't say they wouldn't re-enlist me, they would re-enlist me on a profile, and they'd--I would be on a profile nine and I'd have--and I could not go FMF duty any more or be aboard ship any more. Everything would be strictly state side. And so I--I knew I wasn't a good state side sailor. I mean, I was more comfortable being in the action part of it. So I--they offered me a disability right on the spot. So I took the disability and left the--left the Navy, went back to Minnesota and ran country grain elevators. And I--while I was there, I ran into a friend of mine who had--who was a full colonel in the Army, Army National Guard I should say. And he said well, he said, if you want to stay in the service, I'll get you in the Guard. So I waivered my disability for 25 years more to stay in the--stay in the Guard. And then I worked full time for them for--for the last 20 some years. So I was a civil service technician. I--I--I went through a divorce while I was running the elevator at--at Montevideo, Minnesota. And then I lost my job there because they didn't want a divorced man running the elevator. The farmer's elevator, local type elevator. So I--I went to a little town called Murdock, and I was running the elevator in Murdock when I had the offer to work full time for the Guard, which I did. And I--I done that--I--in those days I come down with terrible bouts of hives. And so I would go to the VA hospital in Minneapolis, and they'd always say well, it's too many tomatoes or too many of this. And so finally after 30 some years of having--having a five gallon cream can full of pills, I said--I said there must be some other reason. And they said no, got to be that. Got to be allergic to something. I said well, I said, have you ever checked my records? And he said yes, I know what the last doctor give you. I said you ever know what the first doctor did? 'Cause that was aboard ship when this happened in 19--in World War II. And so he said no, I've never done that. Well I said read that, 'cause I said, there was no tomatoes or strawberries or anything there. So then he did and he sent me to a--to a--sent me to a doctor who--who did hypnosis, he sent me to an internal medicine doctor. And I went through a series of hypnosis. And the--and the underlying thing was a friend of mine got killed in World War II and I was with him--I was with him when he died. And the last thing he wanted me to do was see his folks and say that--that he was thinking of them. And I--I never did do it. I tried to do it, but I didn't do it. Took his belt buckle, which was all shot up and bloody and everything. And every time I would walk by this dresser, I'd come down with hives. So this man said you got to get rid of that belt buckle. You got to do something with that belt buckle. You got to give it to his folks or somebody. I said, well, I said, I'm sure his folks have passed away by now, mine have. And he said well, he said, you got to give it to a niece or nephew or somebody. So I told this story at a Guard--at a Guard drill one time and two--two of the guys--two of the guys there were deputy sheriffs, Rochester, Minnesota, Olmsted County. And they--one of them called me and he said I was driving by the country and I seen the name Yetter on a mail box, Y-E-T-T-E-R. So he said I thought of you. He said I went in and asked them if they had anyone related to them that was killed in World War II and they said they had an uncle. So he said I got their phone number. He said if you want to talk to them. So I called them. And they said well, we'd rather have you talk to our dad because he was also in the pacific. So I called him, arranged a meeting. His mother was still alive so--to get rid of this belt buckle. And when it happened, I pretty much got rid of the hives. And then after--after I delivered the belt buckle and the hives diminished, then I was turned over to a doctor by the name of Sinnops (ph) in Minneapolic, at the VA hospital. And he transferred me to the hospital in Saint Cloud, Minnesota, and then I was diagnosed there with--with post traumatic stress from Okinawa from the Kamikaze plane. And then he--they said there that to get the best help, you got to go to Topeka, Kansas. So I went to Topeka, came to Topeka, ten years ago in 1992. And I have made a lot of changes in my life. Very, very many. I am now married to a wonderful lady here, and she volunteers out here every day. And she knows this hospital much better than I do. But I think it's a wonderful hospital.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: What else are you involved in here?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I'm involved in the senior Olympics. I've been doing the senior Olympics. I think the first year I done them was in 93 or 4. I think this is my eighth one. And I do the--I do the--I used to swim but my heart went out a time and now I can't swim. But I do the pentathlon, and then I shoot nine ball, pool.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: And do you also keep in touch with--you go to reunions, military reunions?

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Oh, yes, go to reunions. Annd then I volunteer out here, too. I volunteer out here--well, I volunteer most every day and I--and I go to the gym a lot for this knee that's bad. And when I do that, I come back and help Jackie with the coffee run. And I do--what's helped me -- another thing that helped me a whole lot is going to these reunions. I go to the reunions and they seem--it seems like going there, it's kind of a healing thing. Because you're running--you're running into people that you--that you used to know and things--if you don't know the person exactly, if I don't run into somebody that I know personally, I run into somebody that I--that I was in a unit that I know somebody with. So there's always a connection. So I look forward to going to reunions. Okay, that's myself and a corpsman by the name of Brooks. Okay. Now okay. Yeah, this--that's--okay, this picture was painted by my sister, and it's a picture of me wearing--wearing the first mine--the first--the first bullet proof vest, that the first range division got in Korea. This is a letter that I wrote to my brother on a piece of rice paper that we got in--that I got in Japan. We were in there covering for the occupational forces. We were in there before they were because they wanted to make sure that the--that the--that the end of the war was actually legitimate. Okay. This is--this is what the rice paper looks like on the other side. It's strictly a Japanese symbol.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Glenn, it's been very inspiring to hear about World War II and your Korean experience. And I'm glad that you have been a part of this project for us.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: I think this has been a very important project, Kristen. I think--I think it's--I think I feel relieved talking about this. Because this is something you just can't talk about to everyone. And I think when you have an opportunity to talk about it, why, I think you should. I think it's kind of like unloading things. You kind of--it just--it just makes you feel more like you, you know, like you unloaded something. And I--and it's memories that just cannot ever be forgotten, no matter what. And--and I don't think it's bad to share. I think--but I think it has to be done under the right--in the right conditions. And these I think were the right conditions. I appreciate very much what you done.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Thank you. I'm glad that it--the conditions of this project worked for you. Because you're absolutely right, they can't be forgotten and they must never be forgotten. And you have served as great inspiration. And you have once again given of yourself to others, just like you have your entire life and in your military service. And this again goes above and beyond, and it speaks for the kind of person you really are. And it has been wonderful meeting you and your lovely wife. And I feel very honored and privileged. And I'm very proud to know you.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well that's pretty nice words to hear.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: Well, they're true. They're true. So I thank you. If you have anything else in closing, I'd love for you to have the last word.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: Well, I just think--I just think that anybody who has had combat experiences or experiences that are hard to shake, the only way they can shake them is to talk them out. I think--I think--I think it's the way that you--it's a release valve that you have. And I don't think you--I don't think--I think in a setting like this, it's perfect to do.

sp.speaker: Kristin Miller
sp.p: That's great. Thank you Glenn.

sp.speaker: Glenn Ray Sheridan
sp.p: You're welcome.
